The Peace of Westphalia. Two treaties signed in 1648 that ended the devastating Thirty Years War in Europe. The agreements were made in two German cities, Munster and Osnabruck, and they fundamentally reshaped European politics by establishing the principle of national sovereignty and religious tolerance.

Before Westphalia, rulers tried to impose a single faith on their subjects. Afterwards, each ruler could choose the religion of their own state without outside interference. If you didn't like it, you could leave. This was revolutionary for 1648.

The Thirty Years War had been fought primarily on German soil from 1618 to 1648. It was devastating. Roughly a third of the German population was killed. The conflict started as religious, pitting Protestants against Catholics, but by the end, secular power politics dominated.

The treaties introduced a Latin phrase that captured the new principle: cuius regio, eius religio. Whose realm, his religion. That was the deal. And crucially, it established the idea of sovereign equality. States began to recognise each other as juridically equal, not hierarchically ordered under a pope or emperor.

The Holy Roman Empire itself was formally recognised as a loose confederation of independent princes, not a centralised state. This broke the old imperial dominance.

The territorial reshuffling was significant. France gained Alsace and territory in the Pyrenees. Sweden emerged as a major power, acquiring Pomerania and Baltic lands. The Dutch Republic was formally recognised as independent, finally ending Spanish overlordship. German princes gained greater autonomy within the Empire, fragmenting German political power for the next two centuries.

Westphalia replaced religious uniformity with tolerance and coexistence. It also established international diplomacy and treaty law as the mechanism for settling disputes, not conquest. And it created the concept of the balance of power—the idea that multiple states should work together through diplomacy to prevent any single power from dominating.

The Peace of Westphalia marked the death of medieval Christendom and the birth of the modern interstate system. Before it, legitimacy flowed from universal claims by emperors and popes. After it, legitimacy rested on secular territorial control and mutual recognition. This shift was radical. It desacralised sovereignty and replaced religious war with diplomatic negotiation. The treaties are cited as the foundation of modern international law, and the principle of sovereign equality that codified centuries later in the UN Charter traces directly back to Westphalia.
